item.title: The Founder-Led Content Playbook for Premium D2C Brands
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Founder-led content for premium D2C brands across LinkedIn, Instagram, and TikTok. Cadence, formats, and what to actually say.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Founder-led content is the highest-leverage channel a premium D2C brand has. LinkedIn B2B Institute research applies: 95% of the audience is not in-market. Founder posts compound trust across that 95%. The playbook below covers cadence (3 to 4 posts per week), format mix (POV, story, build-in-public, customer), and what to avoid (humblebrag, AI slop).

Customers buy premium from people, not faceless catalogues. The fastest growing premium brands in 2024 to 2025 had visible founders. Not personality-driven, but visible. The playbook below covers what to post, where, and how often without turning the founder into a content factory.

Why does founder content work better than brand content for premium D2C?

Founder content earns trust at 3 to 5x the rate of brand content because audiences attribute taste and judgment to people, not logos. A premium brand is a taste judgment delivered consistently.

Brand accounts post product. Founders post point of view. The point of view is what audiences associate with quality choices. A founder who shares the why behind a fabric, an ingredient, or a manufacturing decision earns more trust than a perfect product photograph ever will.

What is the right cadence?

Three to four posts per week is the right cadence for most founders. Two main platforms (LinkedIn plus Instagram or TikTok), one supporting (the third). More burns the founder; less loses momentum.

  1. LinkedIn. 2 long posts per week. Industry POV plus founder story.
  2. Instagram. 1 to 2 stories per day, 2 posts per week. Visual brand and product.
  3. TikTok. 2 to 3 short videos per week if the audience is there. Talking head plus product.
  4. Newsletter. Monthly long-form deep dive. Most underused channel.
  5. Podcast. Monthly guest appearances. Borrow other audiences.

What format mix should the founder run?

Five formats balance well: POV piece, build-in-public, customer story, behind-the-scenes, and contrarian take. Rotate weekly, do not run the same format twice in a row.

  • POV piece. 'Here is what most brands get wrong about X.' Direct, specific, defensible.
  • Build-in-public. A milestone, a decision, a number. Quietly, not braggy.
  • Customer story. With permission, with detail. The buyer reads themselves into it.
  • Behind-the-scenes. The supplier visit, the lab, the warehouse, the bad day.
  • Contrarian take. Earn attention with a defensible disagreement.

What should the founder avoid posting?

Avoid AI-generated copy that sounds like everyone else, humblebrag updates, vague industry commentary, and engagement-bait questions. Premium audiences spot performance fast.

  • AI slop. Audiences recognise it. Trust drops.
  • Humblebrag. Specific numbers fine, fake humility burns.
  • Vague industry commentary. Take a side or skip the post.
  • Engagement bait. The metric goes up; the audience quality goes down.
  • Daily posting at all costs. Burnout shows. Quality drops.

How do you build a founder content engine that survives a year?

Two principles: a content lead translates founder thinking into drafts, and the founder approves and posts personally. The founder is the source, not the typist.

Most failed founder programs put the founder in the typist seat. The role is wrong. The founder talks, the content lead drafts, the founder edits and posts. Recording weekly 20-minute calls with the founder produces enough source material for 4 posts a week.

Frequently asked questions

What if I am not a natural writer?

You do not need to be. Voice notes plus a content lead works.

How fast does it start working?

Visible inbound demand in 60 to 90 days. Compounding past 6 months.

Should I post on weekends?

LinkedIn no, Instagram yes, TikTok yes.

Do I need a personal brand strategy?

Light one. The strategy is the brand strategy. The founder is the medium.

Will it eat my week?

Three to five hours per week, with a content lead. More without one.

item.title: Wholesale and Retail as a Performance Channel: When Premium D2C Should Open Distribution
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Decision framework for when a premium D2C brand should open wholesale or retail. When yes, when no, and what to negotiate.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Wholesale and retail can either build or break a premium D2C brand. The decision is structural, not opportunistic. Common Thread shows omnichannel DTC brands hit 30 to 45% wholesale share at maturity. The framework below covers when to open, what to negotiate, and how to protect margin and brand position. Done right, retail accelerates growth. Done wrong, it commoditises the brand.

Premium D2C founders ask this question every year: should we open wholesale? The answer is yes, sometimes, with conditions. Below is the decision framework, the trade-offs, and the negotiations that make wholesale a performance channel rather than a margin tax.

When should a premium D2C brand open wholesale?

Open wholesale when the D2C engine is profitable and stable, the brand has unmet demand in regions or formats, and a wholesale partner can reach buyers cheaper than paid media can.

  • D2C profitability is stable, not aspirational.
  • There is genuine demand the website cannot serve (geography, gifting, discovery).
  • Margin on wholesale lands above 35% gross with terms.
  • The right partner is available without a damaging exclusive.
  • The brand can hold price across channels.

When should a premium D2C brand NOT open wholesale?

Skip wholesale when D2C unit economics are still being figured out, when wholesale partners would undercut your own pricing, or when production cannot meet retail SLAs without breaking.

  1. D2C unit economics not solved. Solve there first.
  2. Margin too thin. Wholesale at sub-30% gross is a tax, not a channel.
  3. Production not ready. Retailers will return product if SLAs slip.
  4. Brand still finding voice. Retail freezes the brand in place; do that after, not during, positioning.
  5. Wholesale partner not aligned. The wrong shelf damages perception faster than no shelf.

What should you negotiate with a wholesale partner?

Five non-negotiables: margin structure, payment terms, MAP compliance, marketing co-investment, and a clean exit clause. Ignore any of these and the deal compounds against you.

  • Margin. 45 to 60% wholesale margin to retailer is standard for premium.
  • Terms. 30 to 60 day payment terms; not consignment for premium D2C.
  • MAP compliance. Minimum advertised price enforced.
  • Co-marketing. Brand storefront, training, in-store events.
  • Exit clause. 12 to 18 month review with mutual termination.

How do you measure wholesale as a performance channel?

Track three things: sell-through rate at retail, brand search lift in the partner's regions, and incremental D2C revenue after the partnership launches.

Sell-through at the retailer is the partner's metric. Brand search lift in the partner's regions tells you whether retail is feeding D2C. Incremental D2C revenue (compared to a non-retail region as a control) is the most honest read.

How do you protect the brand inside wholesale?

Protect the brand by curating which retailers, controlling visual merchandising, and refusing the discount cycle. The brand says no to the wrong retailers, not yes to all.

  • Curate ruthlessly. Three good retailers beat ten mediocre ones.
  • Brand merchandising playbook. Mandatory for partners. Auditable.
  • No participation in retailer-led sales below 15% off without prior consent.
  • Annual brand review meeting with each retailer.
  • Walk if the partner refuses MAP or merchandising standards.

  • Meta Ads for premium D2C in 2026
  • The real cost of scaling premium D2C from 1M to 10M
  • Cohort-based CLV modelling for premium D2C

Frequently asked questions

Is Amazon wholesale?

Treat Amazon as its own channel with its own playbook. Different game.

How do I price for wholesale?

Wholesale should not undercut D2C on the same SKU. Use exclusive lines or formats if pressure builds.

Should I start with one retailer or many?

One. Learn the playbook. Replicate.

What about pop-up retail?

Excellent test before permanent wholesale. Lower risk, real signal.

Will wholesale cannibalise D2C?

Some, in shared regions. The math should add up before signing.

item.title: The 2026 B2B SaaS Demand Gen Stack: What Generates Pipeline and What's Theatre
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Honest read on the 2026 B2B SaaS demand gen stack. What actually creates pipeline, what looks busy but does not.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

B2B SaaS demand gen in 2026 has three real drivers and a lot of theatre. The three real drivers: dark social plus brand, product-led content, and tight outbound on a curated ICP. 6sense 2025 B2B Buyer Experience Report confirms 94% of B2B buyers use LLMs in their journey and 70% are anonymous through 70% of the journey. The theatre: gated whitepapers no one downloads, MQL volume KPIs, generic 'thought leadership' nobody reads.

B2B SaaS demand gen has more myth than method in most companies. Below is the honest stack for 2026, split into what works, what is contested, and what is theatre. The split is informed by what we have seen drive pipeline at SaaS companies between 1M and 50M ARR.

What actually drives pipeline in B2B SaaS in 2026?

Three drivers create most pipeline: dark social plus brand exposure (founder content, podcast guesting), product-led content that captures intent at the buying moment, and tight outbound on a curated ICP.

  • Dark social plus brand. Founder content, podcast guesting, community presence. LinkedIn B2B Institute research backs the 95-5 rule.
  • Product-led content. SEO and AI-search content that shows up at decision moments.
  • Curated outbound. 200 to 500 named accounts, not blast outreach.
  • Partnerships. Integration ecosystems, referral programs.
  • Customer marketing. Expansion, references, case studies driven into the funnel.

What does not work as well as people think?

Gated whitepapers, MQL volume targets, and generic webinar funnels are mostly theatre in 2026. They produce activity, not pipeline. The buyer skips past them or self-serves through Reddit.

  1. Gated whitepapers. Most prospects download with a fake email; the asset never trains the next interaction.
  2. MQL volume KPIs. The metric makes the wrong work feel productive.
  3. Generic webinars. Buyers want named experts, narrow topics, and an honest opinion.
  4. Cold email blasts. Reply rate has collapsed to under 0.5% on most lists.
  5. Sales-driven attribution. Without self-reported attribution, sales misses dark social entirely.

What is contested in 2026?

Contested: paid search bidding aggression, LinkedIn lead gen forms versus offsite landing pages, and the value of intent data tools like 6sense and Bombora for sub-100M ARR companies.

Paid search defends brand and captures bottom-funnel. Aggression on non-branded varies by category. LinkedIn lead gen forms are cheap leads of mostly lower quality, lead-gen forms with extra qualification questions perform better. Intent data tools work at scale but rarely pay back below 100M ARR.

What does a healthy 2026 SaaS demand-gen stack look like?

A healthy stack at 5M to 30M ARR runs 4 to 6 named channels with clear roles: brand, organic SEO, paid search, LinkedIn paid, partnerships, plus founder content. Each channel has a leading and lagging metric.

  1. Brand. Founder content plus podcast guesting. Lagging: branded search growth.
  2. Organic SEO and AI search. Leading: keyword wins. Lagging: trial sign-ups.
  3. Paid search. Leading: cost per opportunity. Lagging: closed-won by source.
  4. LinkedIn paid. Leading: cost per qualified opportunity. Lagging: pipeline.
  5. Partnerships. Leading: integration installs. Lagging: co-sold deals.
  6. Founder content. Leading: profile views. Lagging: inbound demos.

How do you build the stack without 20 people?

Most healthy stacks are run by 3 to 5 people: demand-gen lead, content owner, paid ops, partnerships PM, plus an AI ops generalist. Contractors fill design, video, and PR.

Headcount discipline forces channel discipline. A team of three runs the channels that actually create pipeline and ignores the rest. A team of fifteen runs everything and produces only marginally more pipeline.

Sometimes. Gate when the buyer is ready to identify. Ungate everything else.

Yes, on a small named list. Not on a generic intent-data list.

Guesting yes. Hosting only if you can commit two years.

Yes. Brand is 95% of the audience. Skip it and you depend on the 5% in-market.

item.title: Dark Social and the Dark Funnel: How B2B SaaS Buyers Actually Discover You in 2026
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: How B2B SaaS buyers actually discover, evaluate, and choose in 2026. The dark funnel, the LLM dark funnel, and what to do about both.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

B2B SaaS buyers in 2026 spend roughly 70% of the journey anonymous (6sense 2025 report). 94% of them use LLMs to research. The dark funnel (LinkedIn, Slack groups, podcasts, peer chat) is bigger than the visible funnel. The LLM dark funnel (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, AI Overviews) sits on top. Brands that win build presence inside both, not just on their own website.

The buyer that ends up on your demo form has already done 60 to 80% of the buying work elsewhere. The work has been moving from your website into private channels and AI tools for several years. The shift completed in 2024 to 2025. Now, the question is no longer how to track them. It is how to be present in the rooms where they are talking, learning, and asking.

What is the dark funnel in B2B SaaS in 2026?

The dark funnel is every part of the buying journey your analytics cannot see: LinkedIn comments, Slack group chats, podcast listens, peer conversations, dinner debates. It usually accounts for 60 to 80% of the journey.

The dark funnel is not new. What changed: it is now bigger than the visible funnel for most B2B SaaS. Privacy regulation, ad-block adoption, multi-device behaviour, and platform walled gardens turned analytics into a partial view. The buyer learns about you, forms an opinion, and shortlists you before any tracked event fires.

What is the LLM dark funnel?

The LLM dark funnel is the search-and-research workflow that now runs inside ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Gemini, and Google AI Overviews. Buyers ask the LLM for shortlists and shortlist criteria; you appear or you do not.

  • ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and Gemini together processed billions of B2B-style queries per day by late 2025 (Backlinko AI search stats).
  • AI Overviews shows in roughly 30 to 60% of B2B SaaS queries.
  • G2 reviews, Wikipedia entries, Reddit threads, and YouTube videos are the most cited sources (Profound).
  • Branded LLM mentions correlate to branded search lift within 8 to 14 weeks.
  • Vendors with strong G2 + Reddit presence appear in roughly 3x more shortlist queries.

How do you build presence in the dark funnel?

Build dark-funnel presence with founder content on LinkedIn, podcast guesting, a curated community presence, and ensuring G2 and Reddit reviews are real and current.

  1. Founder LinkedIn. 2 long posts a week. Industry POV, not product updates.
  2. Podcast guesting. Aim for 4 to 6 episodes per quarter on category-relevant shows.
  3. Slack / Discord community presence. Useful, named, never spammy.
  4. G2 / TrustRadius / Capterra. Active review management, monthly outreach.
  5. Reddit credibility. Show up in relevant subs with helpful answers; never with links first.

How do you build presence in the LLM dark funnel?

Build LLM-funnel presence with high-quality long-form content on your own site, third-party citations on Wikipedia and G2, and structured data the crawlers can parse.

  • Long-form on your own domain. Definition pages, comparison pages, methodology pages.
  • Wikipedia presence if eligible. The most-cited source in LLM responses.
  • G2 and TrustRadius reviews. Heavy LLM citation weight.
  • Reddit threads with brand mentions. Cited frequently by Perplexity in particular.
  • Schema.org markup. Article, FAQPage, Product, Organization. Improves crawler extraction.
  • YouTube product videos. Cited surprisingly often in LLM responses with citations.

How do you measure the dark funnel without faking it?

Measure the dark funnel by triangulating self-reported attribution, branded search velocity, and LLM citation volume. None alone is enough.

Self-reported attribution at the demo form (a question like 'how did you first hear about us?') routinely shows dark-funnel sources are 4 to 7x more influential than analytics suggest. Branded search velocity correlates strongly with dark-funnel effort. LLM citation volume tracked manually with prompts gives a third signal.

Can I track the dark funnel?

Not directly. You triangulate.

Should I stop using attribution tools?

No. Use them as one of three signals.

Do AI Overviews kill SEO traffic?

They eat informational click-through. Commercial and transactional queries less affected.

Should I use llms.txt?

Yes as low-cost insurance. Spec at llmstxt.org. Do not stake strategy on it.

Will paid still work in 2026?

Yes. It is now one channel among five or six, not the channel.

item.title: LinkedIn Ads for B2B SaaS: A 2026 Playbook with CPM, CTR, and Conversion Benchmarks
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Working 2026 LinkedIn Ads playbook for B2B SaaS. Benchmarks for CPM, CTR, CPL by ICP, plus tested creative and bid strategies.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

LinkedIn Ads CPMs in 2026 land between 35 and 95 EUR for typical B2B SaaS ICPs. Tinuiti and First Page Sage benchmarks put average CTR at 0.45 to 0.85% and CPL at 80 to 240 EUR depending on offer. Lead-gen forms with qualifier questions outperform standard forms. The playbook below covers structure, creative, bid strategy, and what to ignore.

LinkedIn is the highest-quality paid channel in B2B SaaS. It is also the most expensive and easiest to waste. The brands that win on LinkedIn in 2026 run a small number of well-built campaigns with disciplined creative, not 30 ad sets of mediocre material.

What are LinkedIn ad benchmarks for B2B SaaS in 2026?

Typical 2026 benchmarks: CPM 35 to 95 EUR, CTR 0.45 to 0.85%, CPL 80 to 240 EUR for standard lead-gen forms, cost per qualified opportunity 800 to 3,500 EUR depending on deal size.

  • CPM by audience: SMB ICP 35 to 50 EUR, mid-market 55 to 75 EUR, enterprise 75 to 95 EUR.
  • CTR range: 0.45 to 0.85% for single-image and document ads, 0.7 to 1.4% for video.
  • Lead-gen form CPL: 80 to 160 EUR for low-bar offers, 140 to 240 EUR for high-bar.
  • Cost per SQL: 250 to 700 EUR after sales qualification.
  • Cost per opportunity: 800 to 3,500 EUR depending on deal size and ICP fit.

What campaign structure works on LinkedIn in 2026?

A working 2026 structure runs three campaigns per quarter: brand awareness (top of funnel), gated value offer (mid), and demo or trial (bottom). Each with focused creative and audience refinement.

  1. Brand awareness. Reach + video views, focused on ICP definition. Lower budget, longer horizon.
  2. Gated value offer. Lead-gen forms for a research report, calculator, or template.
  3. Demo or trial. Direct conversion ads to the highest-intent landing page.
  4. Retargeting. Engagers from the top two stages, pushed to demo or content.
  5. Conversation ads (sparingly). Mid-funnel only, narrow audiences.

What creative wins on LinkedIn?

Document ads with a clear value bullet, single-image ads with a strong human-led hero, and short founder-led video win in 2026. Generic stock and corporate B-roll lose.

  • Document ads. Carousels of single-page slides. Highest engagement format in 2026.
  • Single-image with founder face. Trust signal compresses qualification.
  • Short founder video. 30 to 60 seconds, talking head, native captions.
  • Customer story. Quote plus number, plus the customer's name and title.
  • Contrarian POV. Earn attention with a defensible disagreement.

How do you pick the audience without burning budget?

Use a 30 to 50k member audience minimum, segment by buying role plus seniority, and exclude existing customers and competitors. Layer firmographic plus skill targeting, not just job title.

Job-title-only targeting in B2B SaaS produces wide, low-fit audiences. Layer industry, company size, and at least one skill or group membership to tighten. Exclude existing customers (CRM-uploaded list) and competitor employees (firm exclusion). The audience tightens from 800k to 80k and quality jumps.

What should you stop doing on LinkedIn in 2026?

Stop running 15+ campaigns, stop using cold InMail at scale, stop relying solely on lead-gen forms without qualifier questions, and stop running on auto-bidding without weekly review.

  • Stop 15+ campaign sprawl. Three to five focused campaigns beat fifteen mediocre.
  • Stop unqualified InMail. Reply rate has collapsed.
  • Stop unqualified lead-gen forms. Add 2 to 3 qualifier questions.
  • Stop ignoring auto-bid caps. Weekly review prevents budget waste.
  • Stop refreshing creative only at end of quarter. Every 3 to 4 weeks for top performers.

How much should I spend on LinkedIn to test?

5k EUR per month minimum for two months. Below that, signal is thin.

Sometimes. Run a 3-month test with a clear exit number.

Should I run conversation ads?

Sparingly. They work for niche, high-fit audiences.

Yes for cold prospecting. Static still works for retargeting.

Should I use LinkedIn's audience expansion?

No. It dilutes the ICP. Keep it off.

item.title: Product-Led Content: How SaaS Companies Generate Demand Without Outbound
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: What product-led content actually looks like in 2026. The structure, the cadence, and the named examples from SaaS brands that grew without outbound.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Product-led content lets SaaS brands generate demand by teaching the buyer to solve the problem with or without the product. Omniscient Digital has popularised the term; companies like Loom, Notion, Linear, and Vercel use the playbook. The structure: build content around use-cases and outcomes, embed the product naturally, optimise for the search and LLM moment the buyer reaches out.

Most SaaS content is product feature articles dressed as blog posts. Product-led content does the opposite: it teaches the problem, names the trade-offs, shows the product solving it inside the explanation. The audience leaves smarter, even if they do not buy yet. That trust compounds across the buying journey.

What is product-led content?

Product-led content is educational content that teaches the buyer to solve a problem the product is built for, with the product appearing naturally as one part of the solution, not the whole pitch.

  • Built around use-cases, not features.
  • Teaches the problem fully, even the parts the product does not solve.
  • Shows the product solving the problem inside the explanation.
  • Indexes for the queries the buyer will run at decision time.
  • Lives in long form on the company's own domain.

Why does product-led content work better than generic SEO?

It works because the buyer's actual question is rarely 'what is X?'; it is 'how do I do X with constraints A, B, C?'. Product-led content answers the second question, the version a buyer will paste into ChatGPT.

Generic SEO content teaches a definition the buyer already knows. Product-led content teaches a workflow the buyer is trying to build. The first wins informational traffic with no buying intent. The second wins fewer visits with much higher conversion.

What does the structure look like?

A working structure: opening problem statement, why most teams get it wrong, the workflow we recommend, the product step embedded, alternatives if our product is not a fit, and an FAQ that answers the LLM-style follow-ups.

  1. Open with the problem framed sharply.
  2. Show why most attempts to solve it fail.
  3. Lay out the workflow that works.
  4. Embed the product step inside the workflow.
  5. Acknowledge where the product is not the right fit.
  6. Close with an FAQ that catches LLM-style follow-up prompts.

Which SaaS brands run product-led content well?

Loom, Notion, Linear, Vercel, HubSpot, Webflow, Intercom, and Stripe all run product-led content at scale. Each one trades short-term feature pages for long-term workflow content.

  • Loom. Async work content beats generic video software comparisons.
  • Notion. Workflow templates beat 'best note-taking app' content.
  • Linear. Engineering process content beats project-management feature lists.
  • Vercel. Frontend deploy workflows beat hosting comparisons.
  • HubSpot. Educational categories at scale; the model many copy.
  • Webflow. Designer-first tutorials.
  • Intercom. Customer support workflow content compounds.
  • Stripe. Atlas + docs as marketing channels (Stripe Atlas).

How do you start a product-led content program from zero?

Start by listing the top 10 use-cases the product is bought for. Pick the top 3. Write 2 long-form pieces per quarter on each. Distribute through LinkedIn, newsletter, and AI search.

  1. List the 10 use-cases the product is actually used for.
  2. Rank by demand: search volume, sales-call frequency, support-ticket frequency.
  3. Pick the top 3. Commit 6 months of content to them.
  4. Two long-form pieces per quarter per use-case.
  5. Distribute. SEO is the lagging benefit; LinkedIn, newsletter, and AI search citations are leading.
  6. Quarterly audit. Cut the topics that did not earn pipeline.

Frequently asked questions

Is product-led content the same as PLG?

Related but different. PLG is a go-to-market motion. Product-led content is a content style.

Do I need a content team?

Two people minimum: a strategist and a writer who understands the product.

How fast does it pay back?

Pipeline indicators in 6 to 9 months. Full payback at 12 to 18 months.

Should I gate any of it?

Gate the high-intent assets only. Most of it stays ungated for distribution.

Will AI search hurt this strategy?

It rewards it. AI search cites educational content over promotional content.

item.title: ABM in 2026: How to Run Account-Based Marketing With a Team of Three
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Practical ABM for SaaS teams of three. The list, the playbook, the metrics, and what to skip from the enterprise version.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Account-based marketing for small SaaS teams is not the enterprise version with less budget. It is a different playbook. Curate 100 to 250 named accounts. Run multi-channel touches per account, not per persona. Measure by account engagement, not lead volume. 6sense data shows ABM-treated accounts close 1.7 to 2.3x faster on average.

ABM is sold mostly as an enterprise motion. It does not have to be. A team of three running disciplined ABM on 150 accounts can outperform an outbound SDR org of fifteen. The playbook below is built for SaaS teams between 1M and 20M ARR.

What does small-team ABM look like in 2026?

Small-team ABM runs a curated list of 100 to 250 named accounts, with multi-channel touches per account, owned end-to-end by a three-person pod (demand gen, content, partnerships).

  • 100 to 250 named accounts.
  • Multi-channel touches per account, not per lead.
  • Three-person pod: demand gen, content, partnerships.
  • Engagement-based scoring, not volume.
  • 30 to 60 day cadence per account; not weekly.

How do you build the list?

Build the list from three sources: ideal customer profile fit (firmographic), buying-signal data (job changes, hiring spikes, technology installs), and relationship proximity (warm intros possible).

  1. Firmographic fit. Industry, size, region, technology stack.
  2. Buying-signal data. Senior hires, job changes, funding rounds.
  3. Relationship proximity. Mutual investor or warm-intro path.
  4. Refresh quarterly. Remove dead accounts. Add fresh ones.
  5. Score and tier. Tier 1 gets the full treatment; tier 2 gets digital only.

What does the per-account playbook look like?

Per-account playbook: research note, personalised LinkedIn outreach from the founder, custom landing page or POV doc, paid retargeting on the company, follow-up sequence on engagement.

  1. Research note. 1-page internal doc on the account.
  2. Personalised LinkedIn outreach. From the founder, not an SDR.
  3. Custom asset. A POV doc, audit, or 1-page landing page.
  4. Paid retargeting. LinkedIn company targeting on the named account.
  5. Engagement signal. Trigger sales call when defined signals fire.

How do you measure small-team ABM?

Measure with three primary signals: account engagement score, pipeline-from-named-accounts, and time-to-pipeline. Forget MQL volume; it does not apply.

  • Account engagement score. Visits, content downloads, demo views by company.
  • Pipeline-from-named-accounts. Treat it like a separate funnel.
  • Time-to-pipeline. How fast a treated account converts to a deal.
  • Win rate on treated vs untreated. Should be 1.5 to 2x.
  • Cost per pipeline-EUR. The honest north-star metric.

What should small-team ABM skip from the enterprise version?

Skip 6sense's full intent data, custom-printed direct mail, multi-week orchestration tools, and persona-based content libraries. The complexity does not pay back below 50 accounts of scale.

Enterprise ABM tooling is expensive and assumes 10+ people executing. Small-team ABM uses LinkedIn, Notion, a CRM, and a spreadsheet. The team is the leverage; the stack stays light.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need an intent data tool?

Not under 5M ARR. Add at 5 to 20M if budgets allow.

Should I use direct mail?

Yes, for tier 1 accounts. High signal, low volume.

Does ABM replace inbound?

Adds to it. Inbound captures self-identified intent; ABM creates intent.

How fast does small-team ABM pay back?

Pipeline indicators in 60 to 90 days; revenue in 4 to 9 months.

What size deal does ABM make sense for?

Annual contract value above 15k EUR. Below that the maths gets thin.

item.title: The Reddit B2B Playbook: How to Be Useful and Get Cited by LLMs
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Reddit is one of the top-cited sources by ChatGPT and Perplexity. How B2B SaaS brands earn presence without being spammy.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Reddit is among the most-cited sources by Perplexity and ChatGPT. Profound research puts Reddit in the top 5 most-cited domains across LLM responses. For B2B SaaS, Reddit doubles as a discovery channel and an LLM-visibility lever. The playbook: identify subreddits, build genuine credibility, answer questions without leading with links, and let the brand mentions accumulate.

Reddit looks unfriendly to brands and is. The brands that win there earn the right to be there. The reward is double: visibility with high-intent buyers and citations inside the LLM responses your future buyers will see.

Why does Reddit matter for B2B SaaS in 2026?

Reddit matters because real buyers research there, and LLMs cite it heavily. ChatGPT and Perplexity surface Reddit threads in answers about category comparisons, pricing, and tool recommendations.

  • Real buyer behaviour. Niche subreddits gather decision-makers.
  • LLM citation weight. Profound consistently shows Reddit in top citation domains.
  • Long-lived threads. A useful answer keeps generating traffic for years.
  • Discovery for niche tools. Buyers ask peer-style questions Reddit answers well.
  • Search visibility. Google now ranks Reddit threads prominently for many queries.

How do you build credibility on Reddit without getting banned?

Build credibility by participating helpfully for 30 to 60 days before mentioning your product, disclosing affiliation when relevant, and leading with substance over links.

  1. Pick 3 to 5 subreddits where your buyers live. Read for two weeks before posting.
  2. Comment helpfully. Answer questions completely, with no link, for the first month.
  3. Disclose affiliation when relevant. Most subs require it. Hiding it kills credibility.
  4. Lead with substance. Links earn the right to be shared after the answer is given.
  5. Build karma. Below 500 karma in a sub, your posts get less visibility.

What kind of content works on Reddit for B2B SaaS?

What works: long answers that solve the asker's problem, honest comparisons (including with competitors), and case-study-style stories without sales language.

  • Long answers. The detailed response gets upvoted; the one-liner does not.
  • Honest comparisons. Mention competitors fairly; trust compounds.
  • Case-study-style stories. Numbers, learnings, what failed.
  • AMAs and weekly Q&A threads. Solid for category leadership over time.
  • Founder participation. The CEO answering directly beats a brand account.

How do you measure Reddit's impact?

Measure Reddit with three signals: branded search lift in the regions where you are active, direct traffic from Reddit URLs, and LLM citation volume tracked manually with prompts.

Reddit's analytics give you the basics. The real signal is downstream: branded search lift, direct traffic, demo bookings via 'how did you hear about us' that mention Reddit, and the appearance of your brand inside LLM responses for category queries.

What should you absolutely not do on Reddit?

Do not: post product links first, run sock-puppet accounts, copy-paste from other subs, or DM users unsolicited. Each of these is a fast ban and a long-term trust loss.

  • Do not post product links cold. Earn the right.
  • Do not run sock-puppets. Reddit detects them. The community detects them faster.
  • Do not cross-post copy-paste. Subs notice.
  • Do not DM users unsolicited. Spam flag.
  • Do not buy upvotes. Recoverable bans turn into permanent ones.

  • Dark social and the LLM dark funnel for B2B SaaS
  • LinkedIn Ads for B2B SaaS with 2026 benchmarks
  • Why G2, Reddit, Wikipedia drive LLM citations
  • How to get cited by ChatGPT for D2C category queries

Frequently asked questions

Can a brand account work?

Yes if it is consistently helpful. Most do not have the patience.

Should the founder be on Reddit personally?

Yes for B2B SaaS. The CEO answering questions beats anything else.

How long until Reddit pays back?

3 to 6 months for visible signal. 9 to 12 for LLM-citation effect.

Is there a paid play?

Reddit ads work for high-volume B2C. Less so for B2B SaaS, which lives in the organic threads.

Will Reddit's API or paywall changes hurt this?

Possible. Build on Reddit as one of five channels, not the channel.

item.title: Marketing Mix Modeling for D2C Brands Under 20M EUR: When It Pays Off and When It Doesn't
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Honest read on MMM for D2C brands under 20M EUR. Revenue and channel thresholds where MMM earns its keep, and where it does not yet.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

MMM gets sold as essential to every DTC brand. It is not, below a certain scale. Measured and Northbeam produce strong MMM for 20M plus EUR brands; under that, the data sparsity hurts. The decision below: when MMM pays back, when it does not, and what to use instead at lower scale.

Marketing mix modelling is the right answer to 'what really drove revenue last quarter?'. It is not the right answer to 'should I cut my Meta budget by 12% next Tuesday?'. Below is the honest scale-by-scale read on when MMM pays back and when it is theatre.

What is MMM?

Marketing Mix Modeling is a statistical method that uses time-series data on spend and outcomes to estimate each channel's contribution to revenue, controlling for seasonality, price, and external factors.

Different from multi-touch attribution. MMM does not need user-level data. It works at the aggregate level. That is why MMM survived iOS 14 and cookie deprecation, while last-click attribution did not.

When does MMM pay back for D2C brands?

MMM pays back when monthly revenue exceeds roughly 1.5M EUR, four or more channels are spending meaningfully, and the team can act on quarterly cadence findings, not daily ones.

  • Monthly revenue above 1.5M EUR. Statistical signal needs the volume.
  • Four or more meaningful channels. MMM needs variation to estimate.
  • Quarterly action cadence. MMM gives a quarterly answer, not a daily one.
  • An owner who can interpret. Someone who knows what 'incremental ROAS' really means.
  • A culture that respects the answer when it disagrees with platform reporting.

When does MMM NOT pay back?

MMM does not pay back below 500k EUR per month, with fewer than three channels, with a daily-decision culture, or without an owner who can defend the methodology to the board.

  1. Below 500k EUR per month. Signal-to-noise is too thin.
  2. Fewer than three meaningful channels. MMM needs variation.
  3. Daily-decision culture. MMM is the wrong tool for daily bidding choices.
  4. No internal owner. Outsourced MMM without an owner becomes a wallpaper deliverable.
  5. Tight runway. The 3 to 6 month payback period may not fit.

What should brands under 20M EUR use instead?

Under 20M, use a triangulation stack: platform reporting plus self-reported attribution at checkout plus quarterly geo-holdout tests. Cheaper, faster, decision-grade.

  • Platform reporting. Leading indicator, biased upward, still useful for tactics.
  • Self-reported attribution. The 'where did you first hear about us' question. Often the most accurate signal of all.
  • Quarterly geo-holdout tests. Causal lift signals on the largest two channels.
  • Cohort-based LTV tracking. Long-term answer to which acquisitions are best.
  • Branded search velocity. The slow-burn truth of brand-building effort.

How much does MMM actually cost?

Vendor MMM lands at 60 to 200k EUR per year for D2C accounts. In-house Bayesian MMM (Meta's Robyn, Google's Meridian) is free in software but needs an analyst at 80 to 130k EUR salary.

The hidden cost is interpretation time. Without an internal owner spending 5 to 10 hours per week reading the model's outputs, the deliverable becomes a PDF nobody acts on.

  • CAC payback and the SaaS metrics boards care about

Frequently asked questions

Is Robyn good enough for a 5M EUR brand?

Yes if you have an analyst. Without one, no.

Should I run MMM and MTA together?

Many do. MTA for tactics, MMM for strategy. Stop using last-click.

How often should I refresh the MMM?

Quarterly minimum. Monthly if revenue is choppy.

Does MMM work for B2B?

It can. But B2B usually has lower channel count and longer cycles; MMM is harder to fit.

Will AI change MMM?

It already has. Bayesian methods plus generative tools for interpretation are the 2026 stack.

item.title: Incrementality Testing on Meta and Google: A Step-by-Step Geo-Holdout Playbook
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Step-by-step geo-holdout incrementality playbook for Meta and Google. Sample size, test windows, statistical significance, and how to read the result.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Geo-holdout tests are the cheapest causal-lift measurement most D2C and B2B brands can run. Pick matched regions, pause spend in one for 2 to 4 weeks, measure the difference. The trick is matching regions correctly and respecting statistical power. Measured's playbook is the most-cited public methodology. Tests cost 5 to 20% of channel revenue for the test window. Worth it 3 to 4 times per year on the largest two channels.

Most teams talk about incrementality. Few run real tests. Geo-holdouts are the lowest-cost causal-lift method available. A well-designed test takes 4 weeks and gives you a real answer about whether a channel is creating revenue or harvesting it.

What is a geo-holdout test?

A geo-holdout test pauses paid spend in matched geographies for a fixed window, then compares revenue in the paused regions to the control regions. The lift difference estimates incrementality.

Different from platform-reported ROAS. Platform reporting answers 'who saw the ad and bought?'. Geo-holdout answers 'would those people have bought anyway?'. The second number is the one that matters for budget decisions.

How do you set up the test?

Setup needs three things: matched regions, a test window of 2 to 4 weeks, and pre-registered metrics. Pick regions that look alike on baseline revenue and recent growth, not by name.

  1. Pick matched region pairs. Similar baseline revenue, similar growth, similar seasonality.
  2. Choose the test window. 2 weeks minimum, 4 weeks better.
  3. Pre-register the metrics. Conversions, revenue, brand search.
  4. Hold all other channels constant. Otherwise you are testing the bundle.
  5. Run the pause cleanly. No leaked spend, no exceptions.

How big does the test need to be?

Sample size depends on baseline conversion volume and the lift you want to detect. For most D2C brands, holding out 15 to 20% of revenue in regions for 3 weeks detects a 10 to 15% lift with 80% power.

  • Below 30 conversions per week in the holdout. Underpowered.
  • Hold-out share 10 to 20% of total channel revenue.
  • Test window 14 to 28 days.
  • Significance threshold 80 to 90% power, 95% confidence.
  • Run on the largest two channels first; smallest later or not at all.

How do you read the result honestly?

Read the result as a range, not a point estimate. Honest output: 'The channel was responsible for X% to Y% of revenue with 90% confidence.' Anything tighter is fake precision.

Platform reporting often shows ROAS of 4x. Geo-holdout often returns true incremental ROAS of 1.6 to 2.5x for mid-funnel paid social. That gap is the platform's pat-on-the-back versus reality. Both numbers matter; treat the platform one as a leading indicator and the geo-holdout one as the true lift.

How often should you run geo-holdouts?

Run on each of the largest two channels every quarter. Run on a third channel annually. Avoid quarterly tests on small channels; the math will not support the read.

  • Largest two channels. Quarterly.
  • Third largest. Annually.
  • Smaller channels. Skip. Use platform reporting plus self-reported attribution.
  • After major creative or audience changes. Re-test sooner if structure shifted.
  • Maintain a results log. Year-over-year trends are the highest signal of all.

Can I run a holdout on Meta and Google at the same time?

Yes but in different regions. Otherwise the bundle effect contaminates the read.

Will Meta let me hold out specific regions?

Yes via campaign-level geo controls.

What about Pinterest or TikTok holdouts?

Possible. Need enough volume per region; usually only at scale.

Should I run the test myself or hire a vendor?

Either. Discipline matters more than the operator.

Geo-holdouts are causal, channel-specific, and slow. MMM is correlational, system-wide, and slower.

item.title: Last-Click Is Dead. What Actually Replaces It in 2026 for D2C
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Last-click attribution is over. The triangulation framework D2C brands now use, with the data sources and the trade-offs.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Last-click attribution gives a tidy answer to the wrong question. In 2026, serious D2C teams have replaced it with a triangulation of platform reporting, MMM, geo-holdouts, and self-reported attribution. Northbeam, Measured, and Common Thread Collective all push the same triangulation. The framework below is the one that works in 2026.

Last-click is intellectually dead and operationally alive in too many companies. The framework below is what credible D2C measurement looks like in 2026, why each layer matters, and what to ignore.

Why is last-click no longer trustworthy?

Last-click never measured causality, but iOS 14, cookie deprecation, and walled-garden reporting made it actively misleading by 2024. It now over-credits bottom-funnel channels and under-credits brand work.

  • iOS 14. Killed cross-app tracking; Meta's reported conversions collapsed and recovered with modelling.
  • Cookie deprecation. Browser changes shrank the visible journey.
  • Walled gardens. Each platform now self-reports with its own attribution window.
  • Privacy regulation. GDPR and CCPA tightened consent flows.
  • AI and dark-funnel research. Buyers identify themselves later in the journey.

What replaces last-click in 2026?

A four-layer triangulation: platform reporting for tactics, marketing mix modeling for strategy, geo-holdouts for channel causality, and self-reported attribution for qualitative signal.

  1. Platform reporting. Leading-indicator level. Useful for daily decisions.
  2. Marketing mix modeling. Strategic level. Quarterly answer.
  3. Geo-holdout tests. Channel causality. Quarterly on top two channels.
  4. Self-reported attribution. Source-of-truth level for true intent.
  5. Brand-search velocity and direct traffic. Slow truths.

How does self-reported attribution work?

Self-reported attribution adds a single question at checkout or demo form ('where did you first hear about us?'). Responses surface dark-funnel sources that analytics misses entirely, especially LinkedIn, podcasts, and Reddit.

Self-reported attribution is the highest-ROI measurement change most brands can make. Cost: 30 minutes of dev time to add the question. Return: a continuous read on which channels are creating intent versus harvesting it. Chris Walker's work at Refine Labs popularised the method for B2B; D2C brands like Magic Spoon and Lalo use it too.

How do you act on the triangulation without paralysis?

Decide daily off platform reporting, monthly off self-reported attribution patterns, quarterly off MMM and geo-holdouts. Keep the lanes separate. Disagreement between layers is signal, not noise.

  • Daily. Platform reporting tells you what to test next.
  • Weekly. Pattern check on self-reported attribution.
  • Monthly. Self-reported attribution rolls up to a channel mix view.
  • Quarterly. MMM and geo-holdout results refresh budget allocation.
  • Annually. Refresh the triangulation methodology itself.

What should D2C brands stop doing in 2026?

Stop reporting last-click ROAS as the headline number, stop crediting the platform that closed without context, and stop hiding self-reported attribution behind sales-only dashboards.

  1. Stop quoting last-click ROAS to boards.
  2. Stop crediting paid social for revenue created by founder content.
  3. Stop ignoring self-reported attribution because it disagrees with analytics.
  4. Stop running quarterly attribution audits as audits; treat them as decisions.
  5. Stop pretending one tool gives a single number.

Is the platform's self-reported ROAS lying?

Not lying. Just biased upward and not causal.

Should I cancel my attribution tool?

Only if you cannot interpret it honestly. Otherwise keep it as one layer.

How long to set up triangulation?

Self-reported attribution: a week. Geo-holdouts: a month. MMM: 60 to 90 days.

Does this work for small brands?

Yes. Self-reported attribution alone is a real upgrade for any brand.

Will AI change this in 2027?

AI will speed analysis. The causal layers stay the same.

item.title: CAC Payback and the Numbers That Matter for B2B SaaS Boards in 2026
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: What B2B SaaS boards actually want from marketing metrics in 2026. CAC payback, magic number, NRR, and how to defend them.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Boards in 2026 want three numbers: CAC payback, magic number, and NRR. OpenView benchmarks put healthy SaaS CAC payback under 18 months for SMB, under 24 for mid-market, under 30 for enterprise. Magic number above 0.7. NRR above 110% for healthy, 120% plus for top quartile. The piece below covers the calculations and how to defend each one.

Marketing leaders that present MQL counts to boards get cut. Marketing leaders that present CAC payback, magic number, and NRR get budget. This is the metric stack that earns trust at the board table in 2026.

What is CAC payback?

CAC payback is the number of months until the gross profit from a new customer covers the customer acquisition cost. The metric matters because it ties marketing spend to capital efficiency.

  • Formula: CAC / (ARR per customer x gross margin) x 12.
  • Healthy SMB SaaS: under 18 months.
  • Healthy mid-market: under 24 months.
  • Healthy enterprise: under 30 months.
  • Above 36: a yellow flag. Above 48: a red flag.

What is the magic number?

Magic number is annualised new ARR divided by sales and marketing spend in the prior quarter. Above 0.7 is healthy; above 1 is efficient growth; below 0.5 means spend is not converting fast enough.

Magic number is the board's favourite efficiency metric because it ties revenue creation directly to investment. OpenView Partners maintains the canonical benchmarks. Trends matter more than absolutes; rising magic number means efficiency is improving.

Why does NRR matter so much in 2026?

Net Revenue Retention measures whether existing customers grow or shrink over time. Above 100% means expansion exceeds churn. The metric is the single best predictor of long-term SaaS valuation.

  • Healthy SMB: 100 to 110% NRR.
  • Healthy mid-market: 110 to 120%.
  • Healthy enterprise: 120%+.
  • Top decile: 130%+.
  • Falling NRR is the early warning sign of product-market drift.

How does marketing influence each of these?

Marketing influences CAC payback through channel mix and conversion. Magic number through demand quality. NRR through customer marketing, expansion enablement, and brand strength.

  1. CAC payback. Drive cheaper, higher-fit acquisitions; improve trial to paid conversion.
  2. Magic number. Tighten demand quality; improve sales-marketing alignment.
  3. NRR. Customer marketing, expansion campaigns, references, advocacy.
  4. Pipeline coverage. The leading indicator the board reads weekly.
  5. Brand health. Slow-burn truth; protects pricing power.

What metrics should marketing leaders stop presenting?

Stop presenting MQL counts, generic 'leads', vanity reach numbers, and content view counts. The board wants efficiency and growth, not activity.

  • MQL counts. The board does not buy them.
  • Generic lead volume. Quality, not quantity.
  • Reach numbers without conversion context.
  • Content views without source quality.
  • Last-quarter-only snapshots. Trends matter; snapshots distort.

  • Geo-holdout incrementality testing playbook

Frequently asked questions

Is CAC payback the same as LTV/CAC?

Related, not identical. CAC payback is months; LTV/CAC is a ratio. Boards care more about the months.

Should I include all marketing salaries in CAC?

Fully loaded CAC includes salaries; partially loaded excludes them. Be consistent.

How often should I report these?

Monthly on the trend, quarterly on the decisioning.

Does AI change CAC math?

It can drop production cost so marketing scales without headcount. Watch CAC stays low, not just the line item.

Will boards still care about brand?

Yes. Brand drives pricing power, NRR, and CAC payback over time.

item.title: Pipeline Forecasting With AI: A Method That Works When Your Sales Cycle Is 90+ Days
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Pipeline forecasting method for long-cycle B2B SaaS. The math, the inputs, and where AI helps and where it cannot.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

AI does not magically forecast B2B SaaS pipeline. A working forecast for long-cycle SaaS uses three inputs: stage-by-stage conversion rates, velocity (days in stage), and a constraint on opportunity creation rate. First Page Sage puts average B2B cycle at 84 to 135 days for mid-market. The method below adds AI for anomaly detection and pattern surfacing, not as the forecast itself.

Pipeline forecasting is where marketing earns its credibility with sales and finance. The method below is the one we use with SaaS clients between 5M and 50M ARR. AI plays a role; it is not the engine.

Why is long-cycle pipeline forecasting hard?

Long cycles produce sparse data, multiple stages produce compounding error, and economic shifts move the conversion rates the model relied on. Forecasts that worked in 2022 broke in 2023 to 2024 for many SaaS teams.

Most B2B SaaS forecasts are wrong by 20 to 35% in a typical quarter. The wrongness compounds across stages and creates board surprises. A better forecast does not eliminate the error; it makes it bounded and explainable.

What inputs does a working forecast use?

Three inputs: stage-by-stage conversion rates (typically by segment), velocity (days in stage), and a constraint on top-of-funnel creation rate. Feed AI for anomaly detection but not as the forecast engine.

  1. Stage conversion rates by segment. SMB, mid-market, enterprise.
  2. Stage velocity. Days in stage by deal size.
  3. Top-of-funnel creation rate. The constraint.
  4. Win-rate adjustment. Discount for current economic conditions.
  5. Quarter-end skew correction. The pattern of pull-forwards.

Where does AI actually help in forecasting?

AI helps in anomaly detection, surfacing deals stuck unusually long, identifying patterns in won-versus-lost data, and drafting the forecast narrative. It does not replace the forecast math.

  • Anomaly detection. Stuck deals, unusual stage skips, oddly fast progressions.
  • Pattern detection. Which features, segments, or sources convert above mean.
  • Narrative draft. The forecast write-up that goes to the board.
  • Reps' qualitative input. Synthesise rep notes into a numeric adjustment.
  • Risk flagging. Deals at risk based on engagement signals.

How do you handle marketing's contribution to the forecast?

Marketing's contribution shows up in TOFU rate and stage-conversion lift on marketing-sourced versus sales-sourced deals. Track separately or the contribution disappears.

Mixing marketing-sourced and sales-sourced pipeline in one forecast hides whether marketing is contributing. Track separately. Marketing-sourced pipeline should typically convert 15 to 25% better than sales-sourced (higher fit), with longer cycles (lower urgency).

How accurate can the forecast realistically be?

Realistic forecast accuracy for long-cycle B2B SaaS: 8 to 15% absolute error one quarter out, 15 to 25% two quarters out, beyond that the error widens fast.

  • One quarter out: 8 to 15% error.
  • Two quarters out: 15 to 25%.
  • Three quarters out: 25 to 40%.
  • Annual: a scenario range, not a number.
  • Track the error itself. Yearly improvement in error is the real win.

Most teams over-buy tooling. Spreadsheet plus weekly discipline beats vendor tools without ownership.

Weekly on the leading indicators; monthly on the full forecast.

Will AI replace the forecasting analyst?

Augment, not replace. Judgment remains human.

What about win rate drift?

Re-baseline quarterly. Win rates move with economy and segment.

Should marketing own the forecast?

Co-own with sales ops. Marketing owns TOFU. Sales owns conversion.

item.title: Multi-Touch Attribution for B2B SaaS Is Mostly Theatre, Here's What to Use Instead
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Why multi-touch attribution rarely tells B2B teams the truth, and what to use instead. Self-reported attribution plus pipeline source.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Multi-touch attribution in B2B SaaS misses 60 to 80% of the journey by design. The buyer is anonymous through most of it (6sense puts the share at 70%). The replacement: self-reported attribution at the demo form, sourced-pipeline tracking, and quarterly geo-holdouts. Refine Labs research has documented the methodology gap for years.

Multi-touch attribution promises a clean explanation of why deals close. It cannot deliver. The buyer's journey lives mostly outside the visible funnel; the tool reports on the visible 20 to 30%. The piece below explains why MTA is mostly theatre in B2B, and what to use instead.

Why does multi-touch attribution fail in B2B SaaS?

MTA fails because the buyer is anonymous through most of the journey, the platforms each report from their own perspective, and the model assigns credit to whatever is tracked, ignoring what is not.

  • 70% of the B2B journey is anonymous (6sense).
  • Dark social (LinkedIn comments, Slack, podcasts) leaves no analytics trace.
  • LLM research (ChatGPT, Perplexity) creates intent that MTA never sees.
  • Walled-garden reporting double-counts and conflicts across platforms.
  • The MTA model assigns credit to visible touches, ignoring the invisible 60 to 80%.

What replaces multi-touch attribution in B2B SaaS?

Replace MTA with three signals: self-reported attribution at the demo form, pipeline-source tracking (with marketing-sourced vs sales-sourced clarity), and quarterly geo-holdout or paid-pause tests on the largest two channels.

  1. Self-reported attribution. One open question on the demo form.
  2. Pipeline source. Marketing-sourced vs sales-sourced, distinct dashboards.
  3. Quarterly channel pause tests. Largest two channels at a time.
  4. Branded search velocity. Slow-burn truth of brand effort.
  5. Customer interview programme. Quarterly, qualitative.

How does self-reported attribution actually work in B2B?

Add 'where did you first hear about us?' as the final question on the demo form. Open text or short list. Most teams find LinkedIn, podcasts, peer referral, and content rank higher than analytics suggested.

Most B2B teams that adopt this find their reported attribution shifts dramatically within two months. Paid search drops from 35% to 18%; founder content rises from invisible to 22%; podcasts appear at 12%. The truth was always there. The tool was looking in the wrong place.

How do you defend the change to a board that loves the old report?

Defend it by showing the consistent gap between MTA and self-reported attribution over 90 days, the geo-holdout result on the channel the MTA over-credits, and the brand-search velocity correlation with the under-credited channels.

  • Pull 90 days of MTA versus self-reported.
  • Run a geo-pause test on the over-credited channel.
  • Correlate branded search lift with under-credited channels.
  • Add a customer interview quote per quarter to humanise.
  • Frame as 'expansion of the truth', not 'rejection of the tool'.

Will MTA tools improve in 2026?

MTA tools are adding AI-driven modelled attribution, which improves the visible-journey read. They do not solve the dark-funnel problem. Expect modest gains, not a methodology revolution.

  • Modelled attribution closes the iOS 14 gap.
  • First-party data deepens the visible read.
  • Identity resolution improves match rates.
  • None of these reach the LLM dark funnel or peer chat.
  • Treat MTA as one of three signals, never the only signal.

  • Geo-holdout incrementality testing playbook
  • What replaces last-click attribution in 2026
  • Dark social and the LLM dark funnel for B2B SaaS

Frequently asked questions

Should I cancel my attribution tool?

Probably not. Use it as one layer. Reduce its weight in decisions.

How accurate is self-reported attribution?

Directionally very accurate. Numerically imprecise. Triangulate.

Does this apply to D2C too?

Less. D2C journeys are shorter and more trackable. But self-reported attribution still helps.

How do I handle multi-stakeholder buying?

Self-reported attribution on the demo form captures the requester. Sales notes capture the others.

What if the board still wants one number?

Give them a triangulated range with a confidence interval. Stop pretending one number is the truth.

item.title: How to Get Your D2C Brand Mentioned by ChatGPT When Buyers Ask 'What's the Best [Category]'
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: How premium D2C brands earn citations inside ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Claude when buyers ask shortlist questions.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Claude shortlist responses determine more premium D2C buying decisions every quarter. Profound identifies Wikipedia, Reddit, G2, YouTube, and Forbes as the top citation sources. Backlinko AI search stats show ChatGPT alone processes 2.5B prompts per day. The work to be cited is real and structural; the brands that do it now will compound the advantage.

A premium buyer asks ChatGPT: 'What is the best premium [category] brand in the Netherlands?'. The model returns a shortlist. Your brand is on it or it is not. The work to be on it is not a sprinkle of llms.txt; it is structural content, third-party citation, and review presence. The piece below is the actual playbook.

Why do LLMs cite some D2C brands and not others?

LLMs cite brands that appear consistently in their training and retrieval sources: Wikipedia, Reddit threads, third-party reviews, YouTube videos, and editorial coverage. Direct site content rarely gets cited on its own.

  • Wikipedia appears in roughly 40% of LLM responses requiring authority (Profound).
  • Reddit cited in 30 to 50% of category shortlist responses.
  • G2 and Trustpilot drive retrieval for review-style queries.
  • YouTube videos cited frequently for product-evaluation prompts.
  • Forbes, Vogue, TechRadar named in editorial-flavoured queries.

What concrete work earns LLM citations for D2C in 2026?

Five workstreams: structured site content, Wikipedia presence where eligible, third-party reviews, founder PR placements, and active Reddit credibility in category subreddits.

  1. Structured site content. Long-form definition and comparison pages on your domain.
  2. Wikipedia. If eligible, a careful editor pass. Cited heavily by LLMs.
  3. Third-party reviews. Trustpilot, Sephora, Marie Claire, Hypebeast depending on category.
  4. Founder PR. Press placements name the brand and rank in LLM training.
  5. Reddit credibility. Real participation in category subreddits, no shilling.

How do you write site content that actually gets cited?

LLMs cite passages that have a clear question H2, a concise answer in the first sentence, and supporting structured data (lists, tables, named sources). Lift-able passages get lifted.

Generic SEO content does not get cited. Structured AEO-style content does. Lead with the answer, structure with tables, name sources by hostname not just URL, and answer the follow-up questions in an FAQ. The piece you are reading uses this structure on purpose.

Which third-party platforms have the most LLM-citation weight?

In 2026, the highest-weight platforms for D2C are Wikipedia, Reddit, Trustpilot or Google Reviews, YouTube, and category-specific editorial (Vogue, Marie Claire, Hypebeast, Cool Hunting).

  • Wikipedia. Highest weight. Hardest to earn.
  • Reddit. Top citation source on Perplexity. Earn through real participation.
  • Trustpilot and Google Reviews. High volume of real, scrapable reviews.
  • YouTube. Product reviews and unboxings cited often.
  • Editorial. Vogue, Marie Claire, Hypebeast, etc. Earned through PR.
  • Substack. Rising. Niche newsletters cited often by Perplexity in 2025.

How do you measure LLM citation progress?

Measure with a recurring prompt panel: run 20 category prompts monthly across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Gemini. Track whether your brand appears, where it ranks in the response, and whose sources it cites.

  1. Build a panel of 20 prompts a buyer would actually run.
  2. Run them monthly across the four major LLMs.
  3. Log appearance, ranking, and source citations.
  4. Track changes over time. The trend is the signal.
  5. Adjust content and PR roadmap based on the gaps.

Frequently asked questions

Does llms.txt help?

Marginally. Low-cost insurance. Not a strategy.

How fast does LLM visibility build?

Source-side work shows in 60 to 120 days. Wikipedia and PR are quarters, not weeks.

Will Google AI Overviews replace ChatGPT for D2C?

Both will coexist. Different audiences. Cover both.

Should I pay for an AI visibility tool like Profound?

Useful at scale. A simple monthly prompt panel does most of the job for under 50M EUR brands.

Are there ways to game LLM citations?

Mostly no. Authentic third-party sources win. Manipulation gets reversed.

item.title: Schema Markup for Premium Ecommerce in the AI Search Era: What Still Matters
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Schema markup priorities for premium ecommerce in 2026. What still earns rich results and AI search citations, and what to skip.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Schema markup still matters in 2026, even more for AI search than for Google rich results. Product, Article, Review, FAQPage, BreadcrumbList, and Organization markup are the priority five. Schema.org Product spec is the canonical reference. Most premium ecommerce sites under-implement and lose retrieval signal as a result.

Schema went from rich-result driver to AI-search retrieval signal in the last 18 months. Crawlers from OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity, and Google all extract structured data when summarising your pages. Missing or thin schema markup is a self-inflicted retrieval gap. The piece below is the working priority list.

Which schema types matter most for premium ecommerce in 2026?

The priority five: Product, Article, Review, FAQPage, BreadcrumbList. Add Organization markup site-wide. Each one improves retrievability by AI crawlers and Google rich results.

  • Product schema. On every PDP. Price, availability, brand, identifier.
  • Article schema. On every blog post. Author, date, image, language.
  • Review schema. Aggregate ratings on PDPs.
  • FAQPage schema. On every page with FAQ section.
  • BreadcrumbList schema. Site-wide on category and product pages.
  • Organization schema. Once, site-wide, in the head.

What does premium-quality Product schema look like?

Premium-quality Product schema includes name, image, brand, GTIN, offers (price, availability), aggregateRating, and review. Anything less leaves retrieval signal on the floor.

  1. name. The exact product name as marketed.
  2. image. Three or more high-resolution images.
  3. brand. The legal brand name plus the marketed name.
  4. GTIN. EAN/UPC where available.
  5. offers. Price, priceCurrency, availability, priceValidUntil.
  6. aggregateRating. ratingValue and reviewCount.
  7. review. Three to five visible reviews per product.

What about FAQPage and HowTo schema?

FAQPage schema is the single highest-leverage addition for AI search visibility. HowTo is heavily used by LLMs for procedural responses. Both still earn rich results in 2026, despite earlier Google rollbacks.

LLMs reward structured Q&A. A page with FAQPage schema gets lifted into Perplexity and ChatGPT responses more often than the same content without. HowTo applies wherever you have a workflow or instructional content. Use both.

What schema should you skip or use sparingly?

Skip Speakable in most cases (limited adoption), skip Event unless you actually run events, skip QAPage outside of community sections, and skip aggressive nesting that bloats page weight.

  • Speakable. Marginal adoption.
  • Event. Only if you run real events.
  • QAPage. Community-style pages only.
  • Excessive nesting. Page weight cost without retrieval gain.
  • Misleading schema. Penalty risk plus credibility loss.

How do you implement and validate schema in 2026?

Use JSON-LD in the head. Validate with Schema.org's validator and Google's Rich Results Test. Monitor crawler errors monthly in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.

  1. JSON-LD in the head. Not microdata, not RDFa.
  2. Schema.org validator for spec compliance.
  3. Google Rich Results Test for eligible types.
  4. Search Console monthly review for errors.
  5. Bing Webmaster Tools for parity.
  6. Spot-check via curl with a user-agent string of the major LLM crawlers.

Frequently asked questions

Does WordPress automate schema?

Yoast, Rank Math, and many themes do. Validate the output; defaults are often incomplete.

Should I self-author or use a plugin?

Plugin for scale, self-author for premium PDPs and high-value pages.

Will AI crawlers respect robots.txt?

Mostly. Use a three-tier robots.txt (allow search, allow fetch, block training as appropriate).

Are there penalties for incorrect schema?

Misleading schema can hurt rich results eligibility. Honest under-implementation is just a missed opportunity.

Does GA4 see schema?

No. Schema is for crawlers. Reporting still runs through GA4 documentation.

item.title: Generative Engine Optimization vs Answer Engine Optimization vs SEO: A Working Definition for 2026
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Clear 2026 definitions of GEO, AEO, and SEO. What each one means, how they relate, and what to actually do.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

GEO, AEO, and SEO overlap and differ in ways that matter for budget. Princeton's GEO study coined GEO. Search Engine Land maintains the working industry definition. AEO is the older term, now mostly absorbed by GEO. SEO is alive and not dead. The piece below sets the definitions and the practical implications for a 2026 marketing plan.

Vendors are conflating three terms to sell whichever one is hottest. The terms have real differences. Below is the working definitional reference. Skim it once, settle the team on a shared vocabulary, and move on.

What is SEO in 2026?

SEO is the practice of optimising content and site structure to rank in traditional search engines (Google, Bing). The discipline is alive, with traffic shifting toward commercial and transactional queries as informational ones get absorbed by AI Overviews.

  • Still drives most B2B and high-AOV D2C traffic in 2026.
  • Informational queries losing click-through to AI Overviews.
  • Commercial and transactional queries less affected.
  • Technical SEO and content quality both still matter.
  • Backlinks still correlate with ranking, less than 2019.

What is AEO?

Answer Engine Optimization is the practice of structuring content for direct answers in featured snippets, voice answers, and zero-click results. AEO is the older term, mostly absorbed into GEO in 2025.

AEO emerged before generative AI search. The structural rules (concise answer, structured data, question-style headings) are the same rules that win GEO. In 2026, most practitioners use 'GEO' to mean both.

What is GEO?

Generative Engine Optimization is the practice of writing and structuring content so it is retrieved, cited, and quoted by LLM-powered search engines like ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and Google AI Overviews.

  • Coined in Princeton's 2023 GEO paper.
  • Industry definition maintained by Search Engine Land.
  • Overlaps heavily with AEO; absorbs most of it.
  • Different from SEO in measurement: citations, not clicks.
  • Requires structural changes: question H2s, answer capsules, lists, FAQ.

How do SEO, AEO, and GEO relate in practice?

Modern content covers all three at once: SEO-friendly structure, AEO-friendly direct answers, GEO-friendly citation-ready passages. The three reinforce each other; treating them as separate disciplines wastes effort.

  1. SEO foundations. Crawlability, schema, internal linking, page speed.
  2. AEO answers. Direct, concise responses near the top.
  3. GEO citations. Named sources, structured passages, question H2s.
  4. Distribution. SEO is one of five distribution channels in 2026.
  5. Measurement. Triangulate: clicks (SEO), featured snippets (AEO), LLM citations (GEO).

What should a marketing leader actually budget for in 2026?

Allocate roughly 50 to 60% of organic budget to content that serves all three at once, 15 to 25% to technical foundations, and 15 to 25% to off-site work that earns citations (PR, partnerships, community).

  • 50 to 60%. Integrated content writing.
  • 15 to 25%. Technical foundations.
  • 15 to 25%. Off-site work for citations.
  • 5 to 10%. Measurement and tooling.
  • Annual: review the split as the channels mature.

item.title: The 7 Content Formats LLMs Cite Most in B2B SaaS
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: Seven content formats that earn the most LLM citations in B2B SaaS, with examples and how to write each.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Across thousands of LLM responses analysed by Profound and others, seven content formats earn most B2B SaaS citations: definition pages, comparison pages, listicles with named tools, original data studies, methodology guides, expert opinion pieces, and FAQ pages with structured Q&A. Each format and how to write it appears below.

Some content formats get cited by LLMs every week. Others get crawled and ignored. The seven below show up disproportionately in B2B SaaS responses; the rest are background noise. Each one has a structural signature that makes it lift-able.

Why do certain formats earn more LLM citations?

LLMs prefer structured, factual passages that can be lifted into an answer with minimal rewriting. Definitions, comparisons, lists, and methodologies all match that profile; loose narrative does not.

The model needs a passage it can quote without adding interpretive scaffolding. The seven formats below each provide that. The opposite (storytelling intros, generic 'what is' fluff, vague thought pieces) provides nothing to lift.

What are the seven formats?

Definition pages, comparison pages, listicles with named tools, original data studies, methodology guides, expert opinion pieces, FAQ pages.

  1. Definition pages. 'What is X?' with a clear capsule answer.
  2. Comparison pages. X vs Y vs Z, with tables.
  3. Listicles with named tools. '10 best tools for X' with reasoning.
  4. Original data studies. Proprietary numbers, with methodology.
  5. Methodology guides. 'How to do X', step-by-step.
  6. Expert opinion pieces. Strong POV with credentials and evidence.
  7. FAQ pages. Structured Q&A with schema.

How do you write a definition page that gets cited?

Lead with the answer in the first 25 to 30 words. Use 'X is a [thing] that [function] for [audience].' Follow with 2 to 3 supporting paragraphs, then a list of features or examples. Wrap with FAQ.

  • Capsule answer in the opening.
  • Two to three supporting paragraphs.
  • Bulleted list of attributes or examples.
  • FAQ block at the bottom.
  • Schema.org Article + DefinedTerm markup.

How do you write a comparison page that gets cited?

Use a table with named tools, real prices, real strengths and weaknesses. Avoid vendor neutrality theatre; pick winners by use-case. State your bias if relevant.

  1. Decide the comparison axes (price, audience, feature, etc.).
  2. Build the table. Real prices, not 'contact sales'.
  3. Pick winners by use-case. Vague comparisons do not get cited.
  4. Add the methodology behind the picks.
  5. FAQ on the most likely follow-ups.

Why do original data studies earn so much LLM weight?

LLMs prefer to cite primary sources. Original data studies are primary sources by definition. A single study can earn citations for years if the data is fresh and methodology defensible.

Most B2B SaaS content is opinion on other people's data. Original studies (your own customer data, your own survey, your own benchmark) flip the citation logic. You become the source, not the secondary commentator. Budget for one or two studies per year; they outperform 20 thin posts.

How should you structure methodology and FAQ pages?

Methodology: numbered steps, named tools, expected outcomes per step, common failure modes. FAQ: question-as-H3, 30 to 80 word answer, schema.org FAQPage markup.

  • Methodology, opening summary capsule.
  • Numbered steps with named tools.
  • Expected outcomes per step.
  • Common failure modes.
  • FAQ as H3 with concise answers and FAQPage schema.

  • GEO vs AEO vs SEO: a working 2026 definition

Frequently asked questions

Should every post try to hit all seven formats?

No. Pick the right format for the topic.

How long should each format be?

Definition 1,200 to 1,800 words; comparison 1,500 to 2,500; data study 2,000 plus; FAQ standalone 800 to 1,500.

Will format alone get me cited?

Format is necessary, not sufficient. You also need authority signals (links, brand mentions).

Do I need to update the formats yearly?

Yes. LLMs prefer recent content. Annual refresh on definition and comparison pages.

Should I add llms.txt?

Sure, low-cost insurance. Format and structure do most of the work.

item.title: How to Audit Your Brand Visibility in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and Google AI Overviews Without Paying for Profound
item.dc:creator: ben
item.excerpt:encoded: DIY method for auditing brand visibility across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and Google AI Overviews. Prompts, tracking sheet, and how to interpret.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Paid AI visibility tools like Profound do great work at scale. Most B2B SaaS and D2C brands do not need them yet. A DIY audit takes 90 minutes a month using a 20-prompt panel and a spreadsheet. The method below is the one we use with clients before recommending a paid tool.

AI visibility tools cost 10 to 30k EUR a year. Useful at scale. Most teams under 20M ARR do not need them yet. A DIY audit gives 80% of the signal at 5% of the cost. Below is the working method.

What does a DIY AI visibility audit need?

Three things: a 20-prompt panel built around buyer queries, monthly cadence across the four major LLMs, and a spreadsheet that logs appearance, ranking, and source citations.

  • 20 prompts that real buyers would run.
  • Four LLMs: ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Gemini (or Google AI Overviews).
  • Monthly cadence. Quarterly minimum.
  • Tracking sheet. Appearance, ranking, sources, sentiment.
  • Same operator each time. Reduces variance.

How do you build the prompt panel?

Build the panel with five prompt types: category shortlist, comparison, pricing question, use-case fit, and trust check. Four prompts per type, 20 total.

  1. Category shortlist. 'Best [category] tools for [audience].'
  2. Comparison. 'X vs Y, which is better for [use case]?'
  3. Pricing. 'How much does [category] cost?'
  4. Use-case fit. 'What is the best tool for [specific scenario]?'
  5. Trust check. 'Is [brand] reliable for [outcome]?'

How do you score each prompt run?

Score on three axes: did the brand appear (yes/no), where did it rank in the response (1 to N), and which sources did the LLM cite. Log all three monthly.

  • Appearance. Binary yes/no.
  • Ranking position. First mentioned, second, etc.
  • Source citations. Which domains did the LLM lean on.
  • Sentiment. Positive, neutral, negative.
  • Notes. Any context that explains the change month over month.

What patterns should you look for?

Look for three patterns: which prompt types you appear in (and which you do not), which competitors consistently appear, and which third-party sources the LLM trusts.

  1. Appearance gap. Where you should appear but do not.
  2. Competitor pattern. Who shows up consistently.
  3. Source pattern. Which third-party sources the LLM trusts.
  4. Trend. Improving, stable, declining month over month.
  5. Action list. What to fix based on the gaps.

When do you need a paid tool like Profound?

Need a paid tool when monthly DIY auditing exceeds 3 to 4 hours, you need cross-brand competitive intelligence, or you want automated alerts when citations change.

Paid tools justify themselves at roughly 30 to 50M ARR or when the team running the audit has higher-value uses for the time. Below that, the DIY method gives the signal you can actually act on.

Yes. Same prompts each month is the comparable baseline.

Yes. Logged-in personalised LLM responses skew the result.

First run 2 hours. Monthly thereafter 60 to 90 minutes.
